outcome: Applications get the strongest factor they can support, and protection is reported by factor type, not a single coverage number.
overview: Multi-factor authentication is widely deployed and widely defeated, because the common factors were designed for a threat model that presumed the attacker was not standing between the user and the login page. Duo covers the ordinary case — a second factor with device health, applied across applications — and, more usefully, supports phishing-resistant factors where the application allows them. The honest way to scope this is by factor type rather than by coverage percentage: an estate at full push-based coverage is less protected than one at partial phishing-resistant coverage.

benefits.text: A second factor bound to a device with a health check is applied across applications
benefits.limits: Push and one-time-code factors are phishable in real time; coverage using them reduces credential-stuffing risk but not adversary-in-the-middle risk

benefits.text: Phishing-resistant factors can be enforced where the application supports them
benefits.limits: Application support is uneven, and the applications that most need it are often the ones least able to take it

benefits.text: Device health can gate access, so an out-of-date device is a policy decision rather than a discovery
benefits.limits: Health checks depend on the device being enrolled; unmanaged devices report nothing and their treatment must be decided explicitly

residency: Cloud-delivered; authentication records are held in vendor-operated regions and the tenant region is recorded at design

notFor.situation: An identity provider whose own second-factor capability already covers the estate with strong factors
notFor.why: A second authentication layer adds enrolment burden and user confusion for no additional protection

notFor.situation: An estate whose critical applications cannot integrate any second factor
notFor.why: Coverage would be achieved everywhere except where it matters, which is a misleading position to hold

Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Cisco implementation partner · Duration: 4–8 weeks to enforced factors across the application inventory

1) Assess — application inventory, current factor coverage by type, device management state
2) Design — factor plan per application, unmanaged-device rule, enrolment approach
3) Roll out — integrations and enrolment by application group, starting with highest value
4) Enforce and hand over — factors enforced, reporting by factor type established, operations handed over
deliverables: Reporting distinguishes phishing-resistant from push and code-based coverage
Every application in the inventory has an assigned factor type and an enforcement date
Unmanaged devices are handled by the signed rule, verified by test
